Learning reusable latent actions from action-free videos offers an effective route to improving Vision-Language-
Action (VLA) policies. However, reconstruction-oriented latent actions do not necessarily benefit policy
learning: as they may encode task-irrelevant static appearance with scene identity, or entangle slowly varying
task progress with fine-grained execution dynamics in limited discrete code. We propose FreshVLA, a
VLA framework built on a frequency-guided, dynamics-sensitive learning paradigm for acquiring temporally

Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy
of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this
assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM
(Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame
alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based
simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders
the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze
the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the
object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the
objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75–0.78,
against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the
simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from
54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing
them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the
real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57%
to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of
MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the
simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees
with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.

Introduction
Action-conditioned video world models take an observation and a sequence of robot actions and render
the future (Yang et al., 2024b; NVIDIA et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025). They must follow the actions
strictly: the arm must move exactly as commanded, an object may move only when the gripper grasps
it, and it must stay where it is released. To this end they are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or
rendered proxy of the scene, such as the commanded robot rendered from its model (Kim et al., 2026), a
4D occupancy sequence (Yang et al., 2026), structural controls such as depth (NVIDIA et al., 2025a) or a
physics simulation (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b), on the assumption that the video will show what the
proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. Fig. 1
does so: with the simulated cup frozen while the arm moves as recorded, one video model leaves the cup in
place, as the proxy does, and another still lifts it.

Introduction
Household robots increasingly execute long-horizon tasks that couple language, navigation, and manipu-
lation (Li et al., 2022; Yenamandra et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025), yet a single robot is bounded by its
reach, payload, footprint, and time. Multiple robots can split a workload or combine different bodies: a tall
manipulator retrieves a mug from a high shelf and leaves it where a smaller teammate can grasp it, or loads a
carrier that transports several items at once. These benefits depend on physical execution: the robots share
access to counters and passages, and a released object can settle out of the receiver’s reach. Team success
therefore depends on collective physical capability: the ability of team members to change the shared world in
ways their teammates can build on.
Existing benchmarks cover parts of this problem. Multi-agent mobile manipulation benchmarks emphasize
task allocation and sequencing through skill-level interfaces (Chang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Dong et al.,
2026; Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2024a; Puig et al., 2024). Physically executed dependencies are evaluated
between fixed-base arms on a shared tabletop (Qin et al., 2025; Mandi et al., 2024), while single-robot mobile
manipulation (Li et al., 2022; Yenamandra et al., 2023; Shukla et al., 2025) and collaborative navigation (Wang
et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026) cover complementary aspects. These settings leave a gap in evaluating whether
a physical state produced by one mobile robot is usable by its teammate in the same evolving scene.
We introduce DeCoNav-Act, a benchmark for language-guided multi-robot mobile manipulation in a shared
physics simulation (figure 1). Tasks are constructed around two coordination mechanisms. In parallel workload
coordination, robots advance separate goals while sharing sources, destinations, and passages. In physical
dependency coordination, one robot establishes a condition for a teammate to use, such as an object released
within reach, a payload settled on a carrier, or a cleared route. Homogeneous teams split workloads and clear
shared space for each other; heterogeneous teams add relays and carrier transport that build on their different
reach, footprint, and payload. DeCoNav-Act contains 350 homogeneous and 150 heterogeneous tasks, each
verified by a continuous joint reference execution, with a 100-task test split.

Introduction
Socially-aware robot person following (RPF) [1–5] is a core capability for human-centered mobile robots in
logistics, security patrol, shopping guidance, personal assistance, and companionship. Unlike generic visual
tracking [6, 7] or obstacle avoidance [8, 9], RPF requires a robot to continuously follow a designated person
in dynamic human environments while preserving target identity, avoiding pedestrians and obstacles, and
maintaining socially comfortable formations. This makes RPF a tightly coupled perception–planning problem:
the robot must track the target under viewpoint changes, illumination variations, distractors, and occlusions,
while simultaneously deciding where and how to move around surrounding people in a socially acceptable
manner.
Despite growing interest in this problem, existing benchmarks only evaluate partial aspects of socially-aware
RPF. Embodied visual tracking (EVT) benchmarks [5, 10, 11] study target following in visually realistic
environments, but mainly focus on keeping a target visible from behind and provide limited evaluation of social
comfort and crowd interaction. Person tracking and re-identification (ReID) benchmarks [12, 13] evaluate
perception in isolation, without closing the loop between target localization and robot motion. Conversely,
socially-aware motion-planning benchmarks such as Follow-Bench 1.0 [14] evaluate safety and comfort in
crowded environments, but assume ground-truth target and pedestrian states in a 2D simulator.

hand trajectories from video. From the same recording, we use each hand’s current pose relative to
the object to represent hand–object affordances. During post-training, we inject these affordances
into the action expert through cross-attention while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen.

tasks, together with converted humanoid action trajectories and rendered robot-view observations.

Introduction 
Weight-space programming (WSP) asks whether a language-model agent can inspect and directly write a 
neural network’s parameters, instead of adapting it through gradient descent. MIT’s initial WSP report [1] 
brought this idea into view, showing that frontier LLMs such as GPT Astra can directly read, edit, and write 
the weights of neural networks to achieve a desired behavior and end goal. This was showcased on vision 
tasks and math problem solving, among others. Within two weeks of the authors’ post, the results attracted 
considerable attention due to the potentially profound implications of WSP. We report the application of 
WSP to robot foundation models (RFMs) and show how failure modes of an RFM can be mitigated without 
additional data collection or training. 
We test whether failures of RFM policies can be corrected through direct weight editing. Our hypothesis is 
that many failures are not random: the policy repeatedly lands in the same recognizable stuck state, such as 
hovering above a target or being unable to reach a target pose. If that situation is recognizable in the model’s 
internal activations, a small edit can use that signal to trigger a correction while leaving the other model 
parameters unchanged. Prior work has directly edited robot policies in weight space. Stranghöner et al. 
wrote state-dependent controllers into unused units of behavior-cloning policies [2]. Other work has edited 
Pi0.5 [3] to change action execution speed [4] or repair instruction grounding [5, 6]. We investigate 
recurring physical execution failures in a Pi0.5 policy. Our edits write task-specific corrective movements 
into the action expert that activate in the diagnosed failure states. Paired held-out evaluations, including 
random and sign-reversed controls, test whether the edits improve performance through the intended 
correction. We also evaluate an edit on a policy already fine-tuned for its task.

Introduction
Video is the most abundant record of how agents act in the physical world, spanning robots of many embodiments,
human manipulation, and simulation. Much of it cannot serve directly as action supervision, since egocentric human
video provides no robot action labels and robot datasets record actions in embodiment-specific spaces. Latent
action models (LAMs) [9, 71, 94] address this gap. An inverse-dynamics model (IDM) infers a latent action from
an observed change, and a forward-dynamics model (FDM) reproduces the change from it. The resulting shared
action space is used to pretrain vision-language-action (VLA) policies [11, 20, 45, 62, 94] and to control world
models [29, 30, 74].
The quality of this space, however, is limited by how it is learned. A typical LAM trains its IDM and FDM from
scratch (Fig. 1a), so the objective trades off pixel reconstruction against the capacity and accuracy of the latent.
Training is also fragile [60, 94]. A loose bottleneck can leak the future frame [71], a tight one cannot describe the
motion [60, 94], and in between the latent drifts toward camera motion or distractors unrelated to the agent [11, 60].
We start from a simple observation. A video world model is natively an FDM (Fig. 1b). Pretrained on large-scale robot
and human video, it carries a strong forward-dynamics prior on how scenes evolve, renders the future faithfully, and
implicitly captures inverse dynamics, which world action models (WAMs) exploit to decode actions [44, 46, 95, 108].

Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on
complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions,
but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how
deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge
coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from
Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics.
Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being
evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across
major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving
overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating
16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing
agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and
agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

Agent harnesses today manage context on the model’s behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers
a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, model-driven context management,
in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models
control over their own context in NOOA, NVIDIA’s open source agent harness, and compared the two
strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K
tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens,
especially at tight budgets: GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget on OfficeQA Pro v2
(21% →56%), and Kimi gains with up to 41% fewer input tokens. Models differ widely, however,
in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and
prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that inference engines can make model-driven
edits cheaper: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, we cut prefill compute
by up to 15% per request with no measurable change in accuracy. Together, these results point
to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that
support KV cache editing.

Large language models increasingly work as teams of agents, and a team is expected to solve problems beyond the
reach of any single member. Most evaluations credit a team for outperforming a single agent, without accounting
for the additional computation: a team may consume many times the tokens of one agent, and a plain vote over
independent answers already explains most of the reported gain. Two questions therefore remain open: When does
interaction itself make a group smarter, and can a group improve its next generation by learning from its own work?
We answer both with the equal-budget ladder, which grades a group against independent agents at three levels:
outperforming a single agent, a compute-matched majority vote, and compute-matched pass@𝑛. On this ladder we
define Recursive Collective Intelligence (RCI) as a group whose own output, without a teacher or external labels,
makes its next generation smarter at equal cost. Three findings follow. First, interaction improves collective intel-
ligence when it moves information across agents: forwarding split facts lifts groups above pass@𝑛at three model
scales, by about a third at 27B. Second, organization emerges spontaneously: identical 27B agents form hubs and
improve accuracy by 18 percentage points; encoding their organization in a prompt enables them to reach level 3
at less than half the token budget in a descriptive comparison. Third, groups recursively improve themselves: Two
label-free generations progressively climb the ladder, the second 9B generation surpassing both pass@𝑛and a con-
trol trained on base-model turns; on PlanBench, HiddenBench and Hanabi, each generation outperforms its prede-
cessor on unseen problems for four to six generations. A group therefore outperforms its members when it forwards
useful information more efficiently than it spends tokens on coordination, and learns to do so from its own work.

During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been
computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard
self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. We introduce Attention Latent Feedback
(ALF), an architecture that allows every sublayer to attend to the outputs of the deeper layers at the
previous position. Training unrolls this cross-position recurrence into two parallel passes, whereas
decoding remains single-pass using cached previous-token states. Across mixture-of-experts models
with up to 4.0B parameters, ALF lowers held-out loss by 0.022–0.024 nats over the standard residual
with about 1.1% decoding FLOP overhead, and consistently outperforms prior final-state feedback
across all three scales on both standard and attention residual backbones. On MoE-1.6B, ALF
matches a 1.38× larger baseline token budget, and on MoE-4.0B it lifts average accuracy across
seventeen downstream benchmarks from 45.1% to 47.0%. Analysis further reveals that intermediate
and nearby deeper layers drive most of this benefit, allowing a fixed nearest-window variant to retain
89%–94% of the gain at linear read cost while learned attention widens its margin with scale.

As code agents evolve, their scope is expanding from generating simple static 3D meshes to constructing
structurally complete, complex, interactive 3D scenes. However, existing datasets mainly rely on

while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT),

Introduction
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) elicits strong reasoning behavior from a pretrained
large language model (LLM) without supervised reasoning traces (Guo et al., 2025). However, RLVR training
can be unstable: a collapsed learner may not recover through continued training alone (Zheng et al., 2025).
Moreover, standard RLVR fixes training configurations before training begins, even though effective hyper-
parameters may change over time. Population-based training (PBT) (Jaderberg et al., 2017) addresses both
problems: it trains multiple agents concurrently, periodically copies the best-performing agents’ weights to
weaker peers, and perturbs their hyperparameters. As a result, PBT restarts stagnating learners from peers
that are still improving and adapts configurations over training. Despite its success in deep reinforcement
learning, PBT has seen little use in LLM post-training (Castanyer et al., 2026).
This work provides one of the first systematic studies of PBT for a population of LLM learners trained with
RLVR on the same task. We introduce PBPT (Population-Based Post-Training), a decentralized framework
that adds an outer loop for online hyperparameter optimization to parallel RLVR training. See Figure 1 for an
overview. Concretely, PBPT uses a shared filesystem as a lightweight communication medium that exposes
the state of the population to all learners. Individual learners train asynchronously and periodically query
this shared state. When underperforming, a learner may reinitialize from a stronger peer through a selection
mechanism. An additional mutation mechanism perturbs training configurations, allowing the population to
continue exploring the hyperparameter space while successful configurations propagate through selection.
We evaluate PBPT on reasoning and multi-turn agentic tool-use benchmarks: Enigmata (Chen et al., 2025),
Nemotron (NVIDIA, 2025), Gaia2 (Froger et al., 2026), and AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024). Across all four,
PBPT outperforms independent RLVR with the same base model, number of learners, and total compute
budget. Further experiments on Enigmata show that PBPT recovers and keeps improving from suboptimal
initial configurations where independent RLVR degrades substantially.

Overview
Feeding each position’s top-layer hidden state back into the next position’s input improves Trans-
former performance.
However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a
drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to
rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-
decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation
error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, State alignment trains
a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model
training untouched. Second, Pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor’s
newly computed state—a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the
verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and
780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within 10−4 bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on
Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4×–2.8× for only ∼2% extra training compute. At large
batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feed-
back’s gains.

Overview
Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence
of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often
collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action,
or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving
a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance.
We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the
proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond
to the robot’s motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back
into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID
dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object
motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual
robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate
object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics
modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.

Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV)
blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget
and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and
couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several
ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and
execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing
thresholds MoBA’s per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata.
KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout
columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task’s loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps
regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these
mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention
across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60× while
raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.

Introduction
Dense self-attention evaluates all pairwise query-key interactions in a sequence, whereas sparse attention
reduces this work by routing each query to only a subset of keys. On GPUs, however, fewer interactions do
not automatically yield proportionally lower latency: score selection, sparse-index construction, irregular
data movement, and load imbalance can offset the savings in arithmetic. An efficient sparse attention method
must therefore jointly optimize the routing decision and the GPU workload that follows from it.
Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) [1] routes at block granularity: it scores each KV block against the
query, retains a fixed number k of blocks, and computes softmax attention over their tokens. FlashMoBA [2]
implements this efficiently, maintaining an ordered Top-k candidate set per query and assigning each CTA a
logical query range whose selected rows are gathered into dense Tensor Core tiles.
Nevertheless, two limitations remain. Fixed Top-k routing assigns the same block budget to queries with
different score distributions, retaining weakly related blocks for concentrated scores while discarding
relevant blocks for diffuse ones. Maintaining the ordered candidate set also adds routing latency. FlashMoBA
organizes metadata by KV block but assigns CTA ownership by logical query range, so several CTAs may
claim one (query head, KV block) column and leave cross-CTA reuse to the cache hierarchy. Coupling
query-group size to k also makes a routing parameter determine scheduling granularity.
